Issued at 240 AM EDT Tue Sep 1 2026

Today-Tonight...Mid-upper level high pressure slides slowly 
eastward from near the Mississippi to the Tennessee River Valleys,
far enough north that mid-level disturbances on the southern 
flank of the high will pass over Florida and the Gulf, helping to 
keep local conditions unsettled. Weakening of the Bermuda high by 
weather systems to the north and anomalously high moisture have 
helped an inverted surface trough develop over the Atlantic waters
offshore Florida, which is forecast to gradually drift west in 
the weak onshore flow. Between the trough and daytime convection, 
multiple rounds of heavy rainfall are possible today and tonight. 
Scattered to numerous showers are expected to develop over the 
Atlantic waters through the rest of the morning, some of which may
move onshore (chances 20-40%). Additional scattered showers and 
storms will then develop along and ahead of the east coast sea 
breeze in the late morning to early afternoon, then push inland 
through the rest of the afternoon and evening (chances 50-70%). 
This activity could get going by late morning. While subsidence 
behind the sea breeze should knock back coverage some behind the 
boundary, the multiple disturbances could kick off yet more rounds
of convection at any point. The trough is forecast to approach 
the coast late in the evening into the overnight, but enhanced 
onshore floor from the sea breeze could move this timeline 
earlier. Scattered to numerous showers will once again develop 
over the Atlantic waters tonight after the sea breeze circulation 
shuts down, some of which could move onshore (chances 20-40%).

Model and recent upper-air soundings show a very saturated 
atmosphere with long-skinny profiles and warm mid-levels (PWATs
2.2-2.4" and T500 around -5 C) typical of an environment 
supportive of heavy rainfall. Easterly steering flow has returned 
but remains weak (10 kts or less), and chaotic boundary 
interactions may again dictate storm motion. Storms or heavy 
showers that become slow/erratic could deliver a quick 2-3" of 
rainfall leading to ponding of water on roads and minor flooding 
of urban, low-lying, or poor drainage areas. There is a very low 
(up to 5%) chance for one or two spots to receive +4" of rainfall
leading to greater flooding impacts, and the Weather Prediction 
Center has outlooked all of East Central Florida in a Marginal 
(level 1 of 4) risk for excessive rainfall. In addition to the 
rainfall, stronger storms and heavy showers will be capable of 
gusty winds 40-50 mph from water loading. Occasional to frequent 
cloud to ground lightning will accompany thunderstorms. If the 
trough settles just off the coast tonight, there is potential for 
training of heavy rainfall and overnight flooding on portions of 
the coastal corridor. Current hi-res models/ensembles don't setup 
significant banding or rainfall, but trends will need to be 
monitored.

As for the rest of the forecast, temperatures seasonable with 
afternoon highs in the U80s-L90s and lows in the L-M70s. Peak 
afternoon heat indices 98-105. A Moderate risk of rip currents 
continues at the beaches. Always swim near a lifeguard, and never 
swim alone.

Wednesday-Thursday...The mid-upper level high over the Southeast 
stalls, then begins to slip back west as the pattern starts to 
amplify in response to troughs/low pressure systems near the 
Pacific Northwest and Southeastern Canada, while mid-level 
disturbances meander over/near Florida at the base of the ridge. 
The surface trough will linger near our coast or possibly have
moved inland, depending how quick it moves today, before the 
Bermuda high strengthens enough to increase onshore flow a bit and
usher the feature westward. This will keep anomalously high 
moisture (PWATS 2.2-2.4") over Florida, continuing the pattern of 
showers and storms developing over the Atlantic waters in the 
overnight/early morning, then shifting inland in the late morning 
and afternoon with the east coast sea breeze. There is potential 
for moisture associated with the remnants of Tropical Storm Dolly 
to add to the soup, though it is becoming increasingly difficult 
to track the remnants, even the moisture plume. The National 
Hurricane Center has dropped this system from the Tropical Weather
Outlook due to very low chances of development. PWATs are already
nearing environment maximums without the additional moisture, and
well above normal afternoon rain chances (60-80%) are forecast 
regardless. The saturated atmosphere will continue to support 
locally high rainfall amounts of 2-3" leading to minor flooding, 
and very low (up to 5%) chances for +4" of rainfall producing more
impactful flooding. NBM is signally an extremely low but non-zero
chance for bulls-eyes over 6", that could lead to flash flooding.
All of East Central Florida remains outlined in a Marginal (level
1 of 4) risk for excessive rainfall both days.
